Abstract
In the era of the Internet of Things, smart devices are widely used in industries such 
as healthcare, finance, and telecommunications, generating massive and diverse 
amounts of data. The aggregation and mining of these data can provide strong busi-
ness support. Still, they also face challenges such as privacy breaches and data het-
erogeneity, which hinder the construction of high-quality personalized models. For 
this reason, this paper proposes a federated learning solution based on cloud edge 
architecture, combines the advantages of edge computing and cloud computing, 
and constructs a personalized model with a privacy protection mechanism through 
condition generation adversary network (cGAN) and parameter sparsity technology. 
Specifically, the model on the edge server is divided into two parts: using cGAN 
to simulate the output features of the shallow part of the model on the edge side, 
sparsifying the local generator and deep network, and then uploading the results to 
the central cloud server. By sharing edge-side generators, common knowledge is 
aggregated to improve local network performance while hiding shallow parts of the 
model. The experimental results show that this method can maintain high prediction 
accuracy while protecting privacy and verifying its feasibility and effectiveness in 
practical applications.

1  Introduction
In recent years, the progress of big data and artificial intelligence (AI) has promoted 
the transformation and upgrading of traditional industries. Data-driven artificial 
intelligence models, such as deep learning, have achieved great success in fields such 
as computer vision, automatic speech recognition, natural language understanding, 
and recommendation systems. Deep learning model training requires a large amount 
of high-quality training data, and the richer the data, the better the performance of 
the trained model [1]. The large-scale deployment of Internet of Things (IoT) intel-
ligent devices has generated a massive amount of data, which is shared by data own-
ers, laying the foundation for improving model performance [2]. Although abundant 
data provide enormous opportunities for artificial intelligence applications, most of 
these data are inherently highly sensitive [3].
Traditional cloud-centric deep learning often requires aggregating data from 
various data sources into a central data warehouse for processing and training. 
However, people are paying more attention to data privacy and security and are 
concerned about this type of data collection [4]. Lawmakers and regulators have 
also introduced many laws and regulations governing data management and use, 
such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [5]. In the industrial 
industry, most of its data reflects the production status of the enterprise and is 
usually collected and stored in isolated form in the relevant departments of dif-
ferent enterprises, and the owners of the data may be reluctant to share the data, 
which poses a great challenge to the application of AI. How to address data frag-
mentation and data isolation while complying with strict and new privacy-pre-
serving regulations is an important issue currently facing AI researchers. Facing 
the irreconcilable contradiction between data-sharing needs and privacy protec-
tion requirements, a solution, federated learning, has emerged [6].
As an emerging distributed learning computing paradigm, federated learning ena-
bles the joint training of superior performance models from raw data without gath-
ering or exchanging private training data among different parties, achieving “data 
immutability and model mobility.” While ensuring user data privacy and security, it 
breaks data silos and fully explores the potential value of data [7]. Federated learn-
ing typically utilizes a client–server architecture to achieve collaborative model 
training for decentralized data, which alleviates the leakage of enterprise data [8].
Although federated learning technology facilitates privacy-preserving data 
collaboration among multiple participants, there is still a core challenge to be 
addressed: once an attacker or a less-than-honest server obtains the model update 
parameters uploaded by each participating device, it may be able to reverse engi-
neer the sensitive data information of the participating devices with the help of 
advanced privacy-invasive techniques, thus raising the concern of privacy leak-
age. This risk directly constrains the willingness of enterprises to share data and 
the possibility of actual operation, because the protection of user privacy and data 
security is a fundamental premise that cannot be compromised.
In traditional centralized learning models, data are stored centrally in a cen-
tral server, which facilitates the model to gain comprehensive insight into data

(1)	 We have designed an innovative federated learning framework that integrates 
cGANs to drive cross-domain model personalization, utilizing model segmen-
tation and sparsity to ensure data privacy. Under this framework, the original 
complete network model is kept locally to avoid privacy risks caused by direct 
exposure to the cloud. This federated learning model architecture can achieve 
efficient, secure, and personalized model training and deployment in industrial 
scenarios, fully protecting the data privacy of all participants.
(2)	 In the model training phase, we first select the client. In the edge computing envi-
ronment, to enhance privacy protection and optimize resource use, we adopted 
an innovative method to deal with the local network model. Specifically, we 
do not directly upload the complete local model to the central cloud server but 
rather segment it at the edge server. By using conditional generative adversarial 
networks, we can generate representative output features from the segmented 
model parts that are sufficient to reflect the key information of the model without 
uploading the entire model itself.
(3)	 In the process of transmitting model parameters, we adopt a data sparsity strategy 
aimed at reducing potential security threats faced by the model. Specifically, by 
applying sparsity techniques, the density of model parameters can be signifi-
cantly reduced, thereby increasing the difficulty for opponents to launch model 
attacks through reverse engineering and other means.

Differential privacy (DP) technology [11] has been applied in privacy-sen-

protect the privacy of local training data and gradient information and can be

a federated feature alignment idea is proposed to minimize the feature distribu-
tion differences between different client data and central server data to reduce 
the negative migration phenomenon in the feature alignment process. In addi-
tion, a federated voting mechanism is designed to fine-tune the global model 
with the help of pseudo-labeled samples to obtain more accurate fault diagno-

method has good application prospects [13]. The DPFL algorithm proposed 
by Shi et al. [14] protects privacy by pruning local updates and adding random 
noise. It utilizes gradient perturbation to mitigate the negative impact of dif-

generated local model.
Homomorphic encryption (HE) allows the data to perform a particular alge-
braic operation on the encrypted content in the encrypted state, and the plaintext 
result of decrypting the consequence of the homomorphic encryption computa-
tion is the same as the processing result of the operation using the plaintext data 
directly. Ma et al. [15] proposed a data privacy-preserving scheme for a cross 
border blockchain network, which utilizes privacy protection technology of 
homomorphic encryption to encrypt on chain data to ensure the “availability and 
invisibility” of on chain private data. Firstly, a cross border blockchain model 
was designed, which detailed the interaction and privacy calculation processes 
in the cross border blockchain model; a distributed private key sharing scheme 
has been designed to provide auditable functionality for relay chains. Ma et al. 
[16] proposed a multi-key homomorphic encryption protocol that encrypts the 
model updates with an aggregated public key prior to sharing the model infor-

effectively counters security threats from within the system. The homomor-
phic encryption-based approach can provide privacy protection. Still, there are 
extremely high computational and communication overheads, which make it dif-
ficult for existing schemes based on this approach to be applied in real-world 
scenarios.

2.3  Application of generative adversarial networks in federated learning
Research efforts in the use of generative adversarial network (GAN) in federated 
learning have focused on the use of GAN to perform data recovery attacks and the 
use of GAN to generate fake data for model training needs [21].
Attackers obtain more sensitive information related to the target based on real-
time interaction during the model learning process and then construct a generative 
adversarial network to affect global performance. The GAN-based attack framework 
[22] can integrate inference technology to infer the private information of other 
participants based on obtaining the global model and even be precise to a specific 
piece of data of the user, with high attack accuracy. Wang et al. [23] proposed using 
malicious server attacks to infer user privacy in federated learning and constructed a 
fusion framework that combines GAN and multitask discriminator, aiming to invis-
ibly recover participant identities and private data. This strategy covertly launches 
malicious attacks to retrieve sensitive information without interfering with the nor-
mal training of the model and achieves good attack effectiveness.
Due to the privacy of COVID-19 data, patient privacy needs to be protected when 
generating COVID-19 data using GAN. Privacy is protected by adding random 
noise to the discriminator that interferes with the original data distribution [24]. The 
private FL-GAN scheme [25] is a federated learning-based differential privacy GAN 
model which enhances the privacy of the system but also affects the model accuracy. 
Literature [26] proposes a method for generating unbiased synthetic datasets using 
federated generative adversarial networks, which generates metadata on an aggrega-
tor using models received from a client and retrains the federated model to achieve 
unbiased image synthesis results.

3.3  Construction of local models for federated learning
3.3.1  Model segmentation
In split learning, a deep neural network is segmented into multiple parts, and each 
part is trained on a different client. The data involved in training can reside on one 
supercomputing resource or be distributed among various cooperating clients. How-
ever, clients do not “see” each other’s data. By segmenting the neural network and 
having each part trained on a different client, data privacy is ensured.
The central server initializes the global model and divides it into parts accord-
ing to a predetermined policy. The client uses its local data to propagate forward to 
the first part of the network, calculating the output of the cutting layer. The cutting 
layer output is then used as input to continue forward propagation of the next sec-
tion. This process is repeated until the forward propagation of the entire network is 
complete. After the forward propagation is complete, the client computes the loss 
function and begins the reverse propagation process. In this way, partition learning 
not only realizes distributed training, but also effectively protects the data privacy of 
each client, because only the output of the cutting layer and the gradient information 
are exchanged on the client, and the original data are always kept in the respective 
client.
In this scheme, the edge server part needs to perform topological steps, including 
dividing the neural network into two separate parts and training iteration steps rely-
ing on local datasets.

4.2  Comparison algorithm
In order to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm and the ability of 
privacy protection, this paper selects the federal average algorithm (federated aver-
aging algorithm, FedAvg) [32], FedProx [33], SplitFed [34], and FedGen [35] as the 
comparison scheme of PPFL. 
(a)	 Federated average algorithm is a classic benchmark algorithm in federated learn-
ing. Its characteristics are reflected in that the cloud server will train the user’s 
model parameter gradient of this round by weighted average and add the model 
parameters after the previous round of aggregation, and optimize the local model 
by using the method of local random gradient descent, finally, the local model 
is aggregated to update the global model parameters as the initialization model 
parameters for the next round.
(b)	 FedProx is an improved federated learning algorithm designed to solve the com-
mon client drift problem in federated learning. In the traditional federated aver-
aging method, the clients update the local model independently, which may lead 
to a large difference in model parameters between different clients, thus affecting 
the convergence and performance of the global model. FedProx alleviates this 
problem by introducing a regularization term that makes local updates smoother 
and reduces the impact of extreme updates.
(c)	 SplitFed is a machine learning framework that combines the advantages of fed-
eral and split learning. The core idea of SplitFed is to split the neural network 
into client side and server side. Specifically: the client is responsible for process-
ing the input data and performing a partial forward pass of the model, typically 
including only the early layers of the model, which are primarily responsible for 
extracting features. The server receives intermediate representations from the 
client, continues with the remaining forward and backward passes, and returns 
the gradient information to the client to update its model portion.

to be solved to meet the requirements of data privacy protection, cope with internal 
and external risks of the system, and optimize the joint training of large models. 
Aiming at the privacy leakage and data heterogeneity problems in the application of 
federated learning to edge computing scenarios, we propose a heterogeneous data-
sharing method with privacy protection, where the local network of each edge server 
is split. The generative adversarial network is used to fit the output representations 
of the partially split network instead of uploading them to the central cloud server, 
which effectively avoids privacy leakage. Each edge server uses the aggregation 
parameters sent down from the central server side to obtain the knowledge embed-
ded in the global generator, which enhances the generalization and accuracy of the 
local model. It is verified through experiments that the proposed scheme can effec-
tively protect data privacy.
Future research will focus on further improving the model performance of com-
bining generative adversarial networks with federated learning. This will include 
exploring new loss functions, optimizing algorithms, and architecture design to 
enhance the effectiveness of personalized strategies. Given the importance of pri-
vacy in federated learning, we will investigate more advanced encryption techniques 
and differential privacy methods. These methods aim to ensure the security and ano-
nymity of user data during distributed training, thereby more effectively addressing 
potential privacy risks.
In the actual deployment of federated learning systems, the heterogeneity of 
devices and data may be more complex than assumed in academic research. For 
device heterogeneity, in addition to performance, it is also necessary to consider the 
accessibility and load-bearing capacity of the devices. In scenarios targeting weak 
endpoints, such as industrial IoT, it is crucial to ensure that local training does not 
overload devices, thereby affecting critical business metrics such as latency. From 
the perspective of algorithm design, it is difficult to completely solve problems such 
as the straggler effect and Byzantine devices through algorithms. From the per-
spective of engineering development, compatibility with hundreds or thousands of 
device models, multiple machine learning frameworks, and different operating sys-
tems undoubtedly brings huge challenges and heavy burdens to user-side program 
development and application configuration. Therefore, customized federated learn-
ing systems may be more suitable for small-scale applications.
In addition to the statistical distribution and heterogeneity of data volume com-
monly assumed in related studies, actual production data (such as industrial data) 
also suffer from issues such as label loss, mixed sample quality, and concept drift. 
These issues make it more difficult to mine common knowledge from multiple data-
sets. Therefore, it is necessary to study how to better measure the training value of 
local data based on privacy protection and explore methods to optimize the global 
model generalization ability under these complex heterogeneous conditions.
In summary, future research will delve into enhancing model performance, 
strengthening privacy protection, and expanding the framework’s application capa-

Abstract: In the era of the Internet of Things, smart devices are widely used in industries such as healthcare, finance, and telecommunications, generating massive and diverse amounts of data. The aggregation and mining of these data can provide strong busi- ness support. Still, they also face challenges such as privacy breaches and data het- erogeneity, which hinder the construction of high-quality personalized models. For this reason, this paper proposes a federated learning solution based on cloud edge architecture, combines the advantages of edge computing and cloud computing, and constructs a personalized model with a privacy protection mechanism through condition generation adversary network (cGAN) and parameter sparsity technology. Specifically, the model on the edge server is divided into two parts: using cGAN to simulate the output features of the shallow part of the model on the edge side, sparsifying the local generator and deep network, and then uploading the results to the central cloud server. By sharing edge-side generators, common knowledge is aggregated to improve local network performance while hiding shallow parts of the model. The experimental results show that this method can maintain high prediction accuracy while protecting privacy and verifying its feasibility and effectiveness in practical applications.
